To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the 40Ar–37Ar age spectrum of plagioclases from the metamorphic breccia 65015 is characterized by a 40Ar plateau age of ∼4 × 109 yr and an older component of ∼4.6 × 109 yr.

the 40Ar–37Ar age spectrum of plagioclases in the lunar breccia 65015 shows a high temperature component with an age of 4.5 Ga, which we attribute with confidence to the time of crystallization of the clast.

the plagioclase in a lunar breccia has a 40Ar/39Ar plateau age which we attribute to its metamorphic history, and that the high temperature fraction of the plagioclases in a lunar highlands breccia has an apparent age of ∼4.6 aeon, which is interpreted as the age of the plagioclast.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of the age and origin of the oldest crustal components of the Moon.
the identification of relict plagioclase grains in a lunar highlands breccia.
the identification and age determination of relict plagioclase in lunar breccias, and with the determination of the age and composition of the early lunar crust.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the ∼ 4 × 109 yr plagioclase age is the best estimate for the formation of the lunar crust.
the 4.48 × 109 yr old component in 65015 represents a fragment of an early lunar crust which was metamorphosed at ∼4.0 × 109 yr ago.
the 4.5–4.6 aeon age of the plagioclase in 65015 is the age of the early lunar crust, which is older than the metamorphic age of ∼4 aeon.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the 4.5 billion year old crust of the Moon is preserved in the form of plagioclases in lunar breccias.
the lunar highlands are composed of a variety of rocks which have been reworked and metamorphosed to a variable degree.
the lunar crust is at least 4.5 billion years old, and that the age of 3 × 109 yr which has often been attributed to the crust is a result of the metamorphism.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the 4.5 billion years old plagioclase grains were not altered by the metamorphic process, and thus represent an ancient component of the lunar highlands.
it is possible for the first time to date relict plagioclase in a metamorphosed highland breccias, and that this age is in good agreement with the ages of lunar meteorites and other lunar samples.
the 4.45 Ga age of 65015 is a robust result.
